lessons.t: Unit 1 · Education for Life (ಜೀವನಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ಶಿಕ್ಷಣ) – Prose: A Day in the Ashram; Poem: Beauty
lessons.words: Gurudeva – Rabindranath Tagore; choristers – members who sing in a church choir; choir – a group of singers; hymn – a song of praise to God; amloki – a tree like a mango tree; reverence – respect; meditate – to pray silently; draftsman – a designer or one who makes plans; recite – sing or say a poem or story from memory; harvest – the time when crops are gathered from farms; sigh – take a long breath when tired; earnest – serious and sincere
lessons.notes: Unit 1 has a prose piece 'A Day in the Ashram' (p. 1–5) and a poem 'Beauty' (p. 14–16). The Ashram in the prose is Shantiniketan, founded by Rabindranath Tagore. Language: Countable nouns are either singular or plural (merchant, friend). Uncountable nouns (truth, peace, milk) cannot be counted directly. Articles: a and an are indefinite; the is definite. Determiners: a few, many, several, a pair of, a piece of, a lot of; demonstratives this/these and that/those. Note: the book prints 'Shantinikethan' in C2 Q2; the correct spelling is Shantiniketan.
ab: ILA – Listen to the passage and answer (p. 1)
1. Why did Sangappa feel sad?
Sangappa felt sad because he expected his son to be studying in a class, but he found that there were no classes and his son was sitting under a tree watching birds.
2. What was his son doing?
His son was sitting on a tree, watching the birds singing and trying to draw them in a book.
3. What did the headmaster say about learning?
The headmaster said that his son was studying nature and learning, whereas the boys who were memorising answers were not learning.
4. Does learning mean only reading books and preparing for the examination? Share your views with your partners in the class.
No. Learning also happens through observation, nature, play, singing, drawing, asking questions and discussion. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 2)
1. Who named the school 'Shantiniketan'?
Gurudeva (Rabindranath Tagore) named it in his song, 'The darling of our hearts'.
2. When does the day in Shantiniketan begin?
The day begins long before sunrise, when the boys are awake and the choristers sing their morning hymn.
3. What is termed by Gurudeva as 'the darling of our hearts'?
Shantiniketan is termed by Gurudeva as 'the darling of our hearts'.
4. Which phrase used in paragraph 1 means 'both the old and the young people'?
'old and young alike'
5. The boys in Shantiniketan get up early in the morning. Who else are the early risers?
The birds (like the birds in the amloki groves) are also early risers.
C2 – Work in pairs. Answer the following questions (p. 4)
1. What kind of work do the boys practise in the afternoon?
In the afternoon the boys practise handiwork such as carpentry, mechanical work, spinning and weaving, drawing or painting, and music.
2. What are Shantinikethan boys famous for?
The boys of Shantiniketan are famous for their sports and games.
3. How do the boys spend their evenings before they go to bed?
In the evening they sit quietly to meditate at sunset; at night fairy tales are told, short dramas are recited, Gurudeva's songs are sung and school gatherings are held.
4. Read the second paragraph carefully. What it describes is: a) the greatness of the teacher b) the song of the choristers c) the lessons taught in the Ashram d) the silent meditation of the inmates
b) the song of the choristers
C3 – Read and discuss with your partner, then write (p. 5)
1. What is the effect of the song of the choristers on the listeners?
The song brings a sense of joy and reverence and gives peace to the soul.
2. How are the classes held in the afternoon in Shantiniketan?
In the afternoon the classes are mainly practical, with work of the hands as well as the mind; there is very little book-work.
3. How do the boys spend their evenings in Shantiniketan?
They meditate at sunset, and at night they listen to fairy tales, watch short dramas, sing Gurudeva's songs and take part in school gatherings.
4. How are the classes at Shantiniketan different from the classes in other schools?

There are no classrooms; the boys sit with their teachers in the open air under trees, in small groups of eight or ten, and learn through conversation, questions and activities instead of dictated notes and memorising.
5. How does Shantiniketan prepare the boys for life?

It prepares them through living education: handiwork that brings out natural talents, games, meditation, freedom to learn, and open discussion that builds confidence and self-reliance. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
C4 – Classify the features into 'living education' and 'unimaginative instruction' (p. 5)
Living education
Meditating, learning outside in nature, open discussion, students asking questions to teachers, experimenting, creative thinking, identifying students' natural taste.
Unimaginative instruction
Memorizing, punishing learners, dictating notes, students passively listening, bookish learning.

D. Grammar – Task 2: Fill in 'a', 'an', 'the' or Ø (p. 10–11)
1. Abdul is ____ excellent football player. As ____ student, he won many prizes. Now he has joined ____ multinational company. ____ company encourages him to play for ____ state level tournaments.
Abdul is an excellent football player. As a student, he won many prizes. Now he has joined a multinational company. The company encourages him to play for (Ø) state level tournaments.
2. ____ Democracy is ____ best form of government, for all ____ people have ____ right to vote. Even in ____ emergency, ____ people do not lose their ____ rights, in that form of government.
Democracy is the best form of government, for all (Ø) people have a right to vote. Even in an emergency, (Ø) people do not lose their (Ø) rights, in that form of government.
3. ____ Peter lives in ____ same locality as I do. His father is ____ Assistant Engineer. He loves ____ music and ____ sports. His most favourite sports is ____ cricket.

Peter lives in the same locality as I do. His father is an Assistant Engineer. He loves (Ø) music and (Ø) sports. His most favourite sport is (Ø) cricket. (Book prints 'sports is'; corrected to 'sport is'.)
D. Grammar – Task 3: Why is 'the' used in some cases but not in others? (p. 11)
1. Man is mortal.
'Man' stands for all men in general, so no article is used.
2. The man going there is carrying a bag. The bag is full.
'The man' refers to a particular person. 'A bag' is used first time (not known to the reader); 'the bag' is used when it is already known.
I'd like to see a tiger. / Would you? Then see the tiger in the calendar.
'a tiger' – first mention, any tiger; 'the tiger' – a particular tiger already referred to.
A. Where is your father? B. He is in hospital. A. Which hospital? B. The Government hospital.
'in hospital' (no article, as a patient); 'the Government hospital' (a particular hospital).
A rose is a beautiful flower. / The rose on your coat is fading.
1. a (any rose, in general) 2. the (a particular rose)
Do you have the tickets? / Here are the tickets. / It is an e-mail. / I have not yet read the e-mail.
1. the (the particular tickets) 2. the 3. an (first mention) 4. the (the same e-mail)

POETRY – Beauty by E-Yeh-Shure: Pre-reading and C1 (p. 14–16)
Pre-reading – What is beauty?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
1. List out the things where beauty can be seen during the day.
The sunlight, the trees, the birds, corn growing, and people working or dancing for their harvest.
2. Pick out any two things of beauty from the poem that are seen at night.
Wind sighing; rain falling (or a singer chanting).
3. Rewrite the other phrases like this: 'wind sighing', 'rain falling', 'a singer chanting'. Why do you think the poet uses the shorter phrases?
Wind that is sighing; rain that is falling; a singer who is chanting. The shorter phrases make the poem brief, musical and rhythmic.
4. The poet says 'Beauty is seen' and 'Beauty is heard.' List out the beautiful things you have seen or heard.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
5. The poet says 'Beauty is in yourself.' What things does she mention here? When does she want us to follow them?
Good deeds and happy thoughts that repeat themselves in your dreams, in your work and even in your rest. She wants us to follow them at all times.
6. Write a paragraph about beauty.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
7. The phrase 'wind sighing' is personification. Give two more examples of personification.
The sun smiled at us. The flowers danced in the breeze. (Any two suitable examples.)

lessons.notes: Unit 2 has a prose piece on Sir C.V. Raman (p. 17–22) and the poem 'The Little Busy Bee' by Isaac Watts (p. 31–34). 1. Where was Bhaskara born?
Bhaskara was born in Vijayapura.
2. Who was his father?
His father was Maheshwaropadhyaya, a learned mathematician.
3. Why do we, Kannadigas, feel proud of Bhaskara?
Because Bhaskara was a Kannadiga, a famous scientist, mathematician and poet, and he invented Kalachakra, the time-clock.
4. Who taught him Mathematics first?
His own father taught him Mathematics first.
5. What is Bhaskara's invention?
Kalachakra, the time-clock.

C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 19)
1. Who were Raman's parents?
His parents were Chandrashekara Iyer and Parvathi Ammal.
2. Why was Raman not able to attend school regularly?
He used to fall sick now and then, so he could not attend school regularly.
3. Where did he complete his Intermediate examination?
He completed his Intermediate examination at Hindu College (Visakhapatnam).
4. What subjects did his relatives advise him to take for B.A.?
His relatives advised him to take History and Economics as his special subjects.
5. Why could not Raman go to the United Kingdom for higher studies?
His health broke down again, so he could not go.
C2 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 21)
1. How long did he work at Calcutta University?
He worked at Calcutta University for fifteen years.
2. What made Raman give up the highly paid post of Special Accountant General?
He gave up the post because he was intensely attached to science and wanted to devote himself to it; he accepted a Professorship at Calcutta University.
3. How did the Soviet Union honour him?
In 1957 the Soviet Union honoured him by awarding the International Lenin Prize.
C3 – Read the questions, discuss with others in the group, then write (p. 22)
1. What makes you think that Raman, even as a boy, had great interest in Science?
He made the model of a dynamo as a boy and borrowed science books from college students and read them.
2. Why did Raman's relatives ask him to take Arts subjects? How did Raman react to it?
His relatives wanted him to take History and Economics because they wanted him to have a secure career. Raman refused, took Physics and studied science.
3. What was Raman's first disappointment in life?
His first disappointment was that his health broke down and he could not go to the United Kingdom for higher studies in science.
4. Why was Raman not happy with the post of Deputy Accountant General?
He felt like a fish out of water in the job; a scientist like him could not be happy with a government accounts post.
5. How can you say that Raman had not lost interest in science when he was the Deputy Accountant General?
He joined the Indian Association of Scientists, got off a moving train to meet scientists, and rushed to see a piece of scientific apparatus in Rangoon.

The poet is speaking about the little busy bee.

The bee sits on the flower to gather honey.

The bee builds her cell very skilfully and spreads wax neatly.

Because the bee is always busy doing useful work, and the poet wants us to be useful too.

Idleness invites mischief; if we are idle, Satan (evil) will find some mischief for us to do.

C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 40)

The walk was pleasant because he could see red and green-roofed bungalows, green lawns and gardens on either side.

The exercise was his daily walk of half a mile from his home to the rail track lines and back.
3. What did the narrator notice one morning?
He noticed two little boys playing in the garden of the more modest cottages.
4. How did the smaller boy behave while playing with the bigger boy?
The smaller (white) boy behaved in a commanding way and ordered the bigger (dark) boy around, while the bigger boy obeyed quietly.

He saw the dark boy commanding and the white boy obeying and doing everything, reversing the roles.

'Get me a banana!' and 'Peel it for me!'
3. Why was the white man surprised at the narrator's outburst?
He was surprised because the narrator suddenly said that the blacks would not rule over the whites and that it was only a game; he had not expected such an outburst.
4. Why do you think the narrator smiled at the end?
He smiled because he understood that the boys were only playing a game and that the man was worried unnecessarily; he felt happy to be in his own country among his people.

C5 – Read and discuss with your partner, then write (p. 44–45)
1. What similarities and differences can you make out between the two boys?

Similarities: both are little boys, both wear blue shirts and khaki pants, both have no shoes and muddy feet, both are sturdy and dressed alike. Differences: one is dark and the other is white; one is bigger and older than the other; their colour and features differ.
2. What three commands did the big boy give the small boy?
'Pick up that stick!' 'Jump into the flowers!' 'Get me some water!'
3. The author could find no answer to some questions. Which are those questions? [See paragraph 5]

Was it that even as a boy he sensed that in his own country he would be at the white man's beck and call? Could he make a difference between himself and the white boy? Could he think that he was going to boss over the black man? Were we, as a race, really inferior?
4. Why was the narrator surprised the next morning?
Because the dark boy was now commanding and the white boy was obeying; the roles had reversed.
5. How did the two boys behave while playing?
One boy commanded and the other obeyed. They took turns to be the boss and the servant, as if it were a game.
6. What made the narrator think that the black boy could be the son of a servant or a classmate of the white boy?

The black boy obeyed the white boy's orders, so the narrator first wondered if he was a servant's son or a classmate; but they were dressed alike, and he was sure the black boy was a neighbour's child.
7. What were the two points that the narrator wanted to clarify to the white man?
(1) The blacks will not rule over the whites. (2) What the children were doing was only a game and should not be taken as a sign of racial superiority.
8. The two boys, though brothers, differed in their colour. What might be the reason?
Children can inherit different colour and features from their parents; the mother was fair brown and the father was white, so the boys looked different.
9. If you were the white man, how would you react to the narrator's comment?

ab: ILA – Listen to the passage and answer (p. 60)
1. Where was the girl at the beginning of the story?
The girl was walking along a lonely deserted road, selling boxes of matches.
2. Why did the girl not want to go home?
She did not want to go home because her father would beat her for not bringing back any money.
3. What did the grandmother do to the child?
Her dead grandmother appeared, took her in her arms and carried her up to the heavens.
4. What could the passersby see after the incident?
The next morning the passersby found the frozen girl lying in the snow with a pretty smile on her lips, and her burnt matches scattered around her.
C1 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 61–62)
1. Where was Oliver Twist born?
Oliver Twist was born in the poorhouse of a little country town.
2. Who were present when Oliver was born?
A doctor who was hastily called and an old pauper woman who was experienced in such matters were present.
3. What happened to the mother as soon as the child was born?
The mother died almost as soon as the baby took his first breath.
4. What did the mother look like while she was alive?
She was a young, good-looking woman.
5. Who was Mr. Bumble?
Mr. Bumble was the town beadle (an officer) who had full authority over the people of the poorhouse and named the baby.
6. How did Mr. Bumble treat the children?
He starved and ill-treated the children under his care.
7. What did Oliver's friends want him to ask the master?
They wanted him to ask for more (food).
C2 – Answer the following questions and share your responses with your partner (p. 63)
1. How were the children fed in the house?
The children were fed in a large stone hall, each child getting a small bowl of watery gruel from the master.
2. Why was 'a council' held by the boys? What did they decide in it?
The boys held a council because one of the bigger boys threatened to eat the boy next to him unless he got an extra bowl of gruel. They decided that Oliver should go and ask the master for more.
3. What did Oliver ask his master for?
He asked for more gruel (more food).
4. How did the master react to the request of Oliver?
He turned pale, aimed a blow at Oliver's head, seized him by the arms and shouted for the beadle.
5. What was the punishment that Oliver got for 'asking for more'?
He was locked in a room alone for the night.
6. What did Mr. Bumble ultimately decide to do with Oliver?
Mr. Bumble decided to get rid of him: a notice was pasted offering five pounds to anyone who would take Oliver off the hands of the poorhouse.
7. What was Oliver's crime, according to Mr. Bumble?
His crime was asking for more food; Mr. Bumble said the boy would be hanged.
C3 – Read and discuss with your partner, then write (p. 64)
1. Briefly explain the circumstances under which Oliver Twist was born.
He was born in a poorhouse on a cold, black winter night in 1837. A doctor and an old pauper woman attended the birth, and his mother died soon after.
2. How can you say that Oliver's mother was a poor woman?
She was found lying in the street, her shoes were torn to pieces, and she had walked some distance; nobody knew where she came from, so she was clearly poor and homeless.
3. What kind of a man was Mr. Bumble?
He was a cruel and proud man who thought himself very great, starved and ill-treated the children, and had no kindness.
4. Why were the boys always hungry?
They were given only a small bowl of watery gruel and never enough to eat.
5. How did the children plan to satisfy their hunger?
They held a council and sent Oliver to ask the master for more gruel.
6. What was the result of Oliver's request for more food?
The master was shocked, Mr. Bumble was horrified, Oliver was locked up and a reward was offered for anyone who would take him away.
7. Why did Mr. Bumble get a notice pasted outside the gate? Explain.
Because he wanted to get rid of Oliver, who had asked for more food. The notice offered a reward to anyone who would take Oliver off the poorhouse's hands.
8. Sum up Oliver's birth and his life in the Poorhouse.

Oliver was born in a poorhouse to a young mother who died soon after. He was named by Mr. Bumble and grew up hungry, ill-treated, unloved, with only miserable companions. He was finally punished for asking for more food.
9. Briefly narrate the events that led to Oliver being locked up in a room.

The boys were always hungry. One bigger boy threatened to eat his neighbour unless he got more gruel. The boys held a council and forced Oliver to ask the master for more. The master was shocked and called Mr. Bumble, who punished Oliver by locking him up.

b. The briefcase was stolen at the station. (Where)

D. Writing – Write a paragraph based on the table about Ruskin Bond (p. 71)
Task 1 – Write a paragraph using the given facts about Ruskin Bond.

Ruskin Bond, a famous novelist and story writer, was born in Kasuli, Himachal Pradesh on 19 May 1934. He stays in Mussoorie. He is the author of many books that have been translated into many European and Indian languages. Ruskin Bond was awarded the Kendra Sahitya Akademi Award in 1992.
POETRY – For a Five Year Old by Fleur Adcock: C1 and C2 (p. 72–73)
C1 – 1. Name the creature mentioned in the poem.
A snail.
C1 – 2. Who do you think is the speaker?
The mother is the speaker.
C1 – 3. Who is the speaker addressing?
The speaker is addressing her five-year-old child.
C1 – 4. What does the child want his mother to see?
The child wants his mother to see the snail climbing up the windowsill.
C1 – 5. What does the mother tell the child?
She tells the child that it would be unkind to leave the snail there, so they must carry it outside to eat a daffodil; they must be kind to snails.
C2 – 1. Why does the mother say 'a kind of faith prevails'?
She means it is commonly believed that a child's character is built more by words of advice than by what adults actually do; she realises that her own words are not matched by her actions.
C2 – 2. How has the mother treated other animals?
She has trapped mice, shot wild birds and drowned kittens.
C2 – 3. Do you observe any difference between the mother's treatment of the snail and her treatment of other animals and her own relatives?
Yes. She is gentle and kind to the snail but has been cruel to other animals, and has betrayed and been harsh with her relatives.
C2 – 4. How does the mother console herself? Read the last two lines and comment.

She consoles herself with the thought that she is at least kind to snails and that she is still her child's mother. The line shows her acceptance of her own faults along with her wish to teach kindness.

lessons.au: From the Mahabharatha (Dharmavyadha); Folk tale (The Earthquake)
lessons.words: proficient – learned; surpass – beat; stunned – shocked; depressed – very sad; grief – sorrow; cultivate – learn; bestowed – given; virtue – good quality; hereditary – inherited by birth; glared – looked at with anger; confounded – confused; forsaking – leaving; perched – sat; dwelt – thought; wrath – anger; ascetic – divine; alms – food or gifts given to the poor; startled – surprised; mysteries – secrets; chaste – pure, religious; conceit – false pride; sir – teacher, a word of respect; inherent duty – primary duty; shield – defence; elated – overjoyed; shrub – bush; habitat – place of living; terrified – afraid very much; shivering – shaking with fear; fleeing – running away; gazelle – small-eyed antelope; stampede – a mad rush; wild flight – running with great fear; huddled – crowded together; species – a group of animals able to breed with each other; crash – a sudden loud noise; crack up – split; not daring – not having courage
lessons.notes: The Supplementary Reader has two stories: 'The Story of Dharmavyadha' from the Mahabharatha (p. 76–78) and 'The Earthquake', a folk tale (p. 79–82). Exercises: Part I – answer in a sentence or two; Part II – answer in a paragraph or in about 50–60 words. Lesson: the value of humility, respect for parents, and not believing rumours without checking the facts.
ab: Dharmavyadha – I. Answer each of the following in a sentence or two (p. 78)
1. Why was Kaushika very angry with the bird?
The crane was twittering loudly and disturbing his studies, so he glared at it in anger and it was reduced to ashes.
2. Why did the housewife delay in giving alms to Kaushika?
She was attending to her husband who had just come home, so she took some time to bring the alms.
3. Who did she advise Kaushika to meet?
She advised him to meet Dharmavyadha in the city of Mithila.
4. Why did Kaushika feel stunned at the words of Dharmavyadha?
Dharmavyadha said that the chaste woman had sent him, which meant that the woman had known about the crane and that the butcher was also wise; Kaushika realised he was not the only learned man.
5. What did Kaushika do after his visit to Dharmavyadha?
He returned home, served his aged parents and taught others the Vedic lore he had mastered.
6. What did Sage Markandeya tell Yudhishtira in the end?
He said that in every division of people there are enlightened souls who can guide even scholars and masters of the Vedic teachings.
Dharmavyadha – II. Answer each of the following in a paragraph (p. 78)
1. Narrate how Kaushika felt on listening to the lady.

Kaushika was startled and confused when the lady knew that he had killed the crane with his glare. He wondered how she knew, and felt that he was not as learned as he thought. Her words made him curious to meet Dharmavyadha. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
2. What are the essentials of Dharma, according to Dharmavyadha?

To do one's duty, to be truthful, patient and merciful, not to be overjoyed in happiness or depressed in difficulties, to pray and practise penance, to appreciate others' good qualities, not to boast, to bathe in sacred rivers, visit holy places, and serve our parents and our teacher.
3. What can we learn from the story of Dharmavyadha?

We learn that knowledge should be combined with humility, that true Dharma includes truth, duty and service to parents, and that wise people can be found in every walk of life. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
The Earthquake – I. Answer each of the following in a sentence or two (p. 82)
1. What was the wild imagination of the hare?
The hare imagined that the earth was falling to pieces when a ripe bel fruit fell on the palm shrub.
2. Which event caused the crash?
A ripe bel fruit fell on top of the palm shrub, causing the crash.
3. Name a few animals that joined the race.
Deer, boar, antelope, buffalo, gazelle, rhinoceros, tiger and elephant (any few).
4. Which of the animals do you think was the sensible one? How do you justify that?
The lion was the sensible one, because he did not believe the rumour without checking; he went to see the place himself and found the real cause.
5. What did the lion guess about the cause of the crash?
He guessed that a ripe bel fruit had fallen on the palm leaf and made the crash, and that the hare had mistaken it for an earthquake.
6. What was the command given by the lion to the animals at the end?
'Go back to your places, and live as you did before.'
The Earthquake – II. Write the answers in about 50–60 words (p. 82)
1. It is said: 'The mob cannot think.' Do you agree? If so, how does this story illustrate that? If you do not agree, how do you explain the behaviour of the animals?

I agree. The animals ran in a mad stampede simply because one hare said that the earth was falling to pieces. None of them stopped to check the facts; each asked another and followed the crowd. Only the lion's thinking and his checking the truth saved them from needless panic. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
2. Sum up what the lion did to verify the statement of the hare.

The lion asked all the animals who had told them, and was led to the hare. He then took the hare to the palm trees and examined the spot. He found a ripe bel fruit had fallen on the palm shrub, realised that there was no earthquake, and then told all the animals the truth so that they could return to their homes.
